extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; literary critics; creative poets interested in aesthetic criteria
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-aesthetic criteria and standards for judging poetry and art (especially Renaissance poetry and Winckelmannian art-criticism): music, form, originality, sincerity, country-rootedness, learnedness, refinement, influence, and related qualities. The page discusses what gives poems and criticism historical interest versus enduring aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic of an age / 'poetry a la mode'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may derive interest from being 'part of the manner of a time' — a decoration of an age, valued as a specimen of contemporary taste rather than as an expression of unique individual genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such work is historically interesting because it exemplifies the aesthetic conditions and fashions of its era ("one of the decorations of an age which threw much of its energy into the work of decoration"). Its value can be largely documentary or sociological rather than purely aesthetic; one should judge whether interest is historical (typical of an age) or individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality / originality of temper
rubrics_metrics.description: For the highest interest, a poet must show "something individual, inventive, unique, the impress ... of the writer's own temper and personality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conforming to an age's manner is not sufficient; critics should look for the personal stamp or invention that lifts work from historical curiosity to enduring aesthetic value (example contrast between being 'true child of his age' and possessing 'an impress of the writer's own temper').

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality / 'double music' (metrical and rhymed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition to unite the measured, scanned verse of Latin/Greek with the rhymed, unscanned older French verse to produce a 'double music'—harmonising the measure of every syllable with rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the poem's ear: its metrical rigour, use of rhyme, and ability to combine different musical traditions. The Pleiad's obsession with music ("insatiable of music") is central to their aesthetic; examples include setting of songs to music (Goudimel) and searching for exquisite, various musical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learnedness / erudition (and pedantry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may display 'quaint, remote learning'—concern with orthography, classical spellings, Greek words, and even coined terms—sometimes leading to a slight pedantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such erudition can contribute charm and foreign elegance but may also be ephemeral or alienating (foreign words that 'had only an ephemeral existence'). Evaluate whether learnedness enriches or obscures the poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / sincerity of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional authenticity matters—whether love and grief feel real or are merely fashionable affectations (the Pleiad's 'loves are only half real'). Conversely, 'poesie intime' aims at portraiture of the writer's most intimate moods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish affectation and courtly posturing from genuine intimate expression (Du Bellay's Regrets as an example of 'poesie intime'). Authenticity often produces deeper and more lasting resonance than mannered sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation versus substance (decorative imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ornament, diminutives, and playful myth can be delightful but may make poetry primarily decorative—imagery of death used as 'delicate ornament' or grotesques nestling with flowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether ornament is serving a deeper aim or merely delightful surface decoration; recognise both the pleasure of ornament and its potential shallowness when it substitutes for substantive feeling or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish, grace, and refinement of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit in "grace and finish, perfect in minute detail"—a subtle, exquisite faintness and refinement achieved by long study and reiterated refinements rather than force or originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate craftsmanship: careful finishing, delicate touches, and polished detail can be high virtues, especially for an audience that values refinement over vehemence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience / exclusivity of address
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poetry is 'not for the people, but for a confined circle'—courtiers, erudite persons, or those seeking refined voluptuousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whom the poem is intended to please: popular accessibility versus cultivated exclusivity affects both style and method. Evaluate success relative to the intended circle rather than absolute popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rootedness in country / local colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'true to its country' uses recurring names, scenery, and regional traits (Loire, La Beauce, upland country) — landscape and domestic life form part of aesthetic identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how convincingly a work evokes place and how such rootedness contributes to its character and mood (domesticity, homeliness, winter-pleasures, fireside imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of landscape and ruins / sentiment for antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: A modern feeling includes love of landscape and 'the sentiment of ruins'—a melancholic appreciation of transience and the 'grandeur of nothingness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poets who can translate landscape and ruins into a personal, elegiac sensibility (nostalgia, homesickness, longing) that deepens the work's affective range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form over matter / mastery of poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: In some great poems 'the matter is almost nothing, and the form almost everything'—the poet's distinctive formal shaping (language, stanza, voice) is the primary source of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the originality and control of form: tight formal invention can make trivial subject-matter memorable (Du Bellay's handling of old French form in his poem is given as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and subtlety / transfiguration of the trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to transfigure slight, trivial incidents by a sudden light or deft handling so that a 'pure effect' yields lasting relish despite its fleetingness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for economy—small subjects treated with craft that produce a poignant or delicate effect without brute emphasis (e.g., a winnower's song, dust in barn door).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-minded intellectual integrity / fidelity to one's motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrity and truth to one's type: a severe, narrow perfection achieved by pursuing a single supreme motive without dilution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the moral and aesthetic integrity of a focused artist or critic (Winckelmann's 'feverish nursing of the one motive') while recognising this as a deliberate trade-off against versatility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative influence / initiating new sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical or artistic work may be judged by its capacity to 'lay open a new organ for the human spirit'—to initiate a new sense or way of seeing (Winckelmann's initiation of a new organ for art-study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether work creates lasting critical or aesthetic consequences beyond its immediate merits—whether it opens fresh perception or alters subsequent culture ('One learns nothing from him, but one becomes something').

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated taste / higher sensibility for art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'beauty of art demands a higher sensibility than the beauty of nature' and must be awakened and repaired by culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should probe whether a reader's cultivated sensibility is required to apprehend the work; works that presuppose or cultivate refined taste may be judged on how successfully they develop that sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct sensory engagement vs abstract theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for escaping 'abstract theory' toward intuition and the 'exercise of sight and touch'—direct handling and perception of art rather than over-theorising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value criticism and creation that ground themselves in palpable, sensory apprehension (drawing from the antique, tactile study) rather than merely philosophical abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and renunciation (focus versus versatility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic path often requires choosing a specialization and renouncing other crowns—there is a tension between initiating a new focused organ and cultivating multiple types of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, consider whether a creator's renunciation and chosen focus are justified by the depth and distinctness of the resulting work; both concentrated single-mindedness and broad cultivation are legitimate, but different, virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for posterity / striving for lasting worth
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's declared aspiration to be acknowledged by posterity ('It will be my highest reward, if posterity acknowledges that I have written worthily').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should consider whether the work aspires to, and achieves, qualities (originality, depth, form) likely to outlast contemporary fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of critical or artistic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with a direct, programmatic purpose (e.g., an appeal against artificial classicism to the study of the antique) is to be judged for the force and clarity of that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how clearly a work defines its aims and how coherently it pursues them; programmatic clarity can be a virtue in both criticism and artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and breadth of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: True taste requires impartiality (not being moved by only one type of beauty); those moved by beauty in only one gender or aspect may lack an 'impartial, vital, inborn instinct for beauty in art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the critic/artist cultivates an open, broad sensibility able to apprehend diverse forms of beauty (e.g., appreciation of male as well as female beauty in Greek art).
